Johannes Wollebius
yoh-HAH-nuhs voh-LEE-bee-uhs
proper noun (person)
Swiss Reformed theologian (1589-1629) of Basel, author of the widely used Compendium of Christian Theology.

📖 Biblical Definition

Johannes Wollebius was a Swiss Reformed theologian of Basel, author of the Compendium Theologiae Christianae, one of the most concise, orderly, and widely used handbooks of Reformed theology in the seventeenth century. Where larger systems sprawled across many volumes, Wollebius distilled the whole of Christian doctrine into a clear, well-ordered summary, arranging it under the knowledge of God and the worship of God, and marking out the heads of doctrine with such precision that students across Europe and even in early New England learned their theology from him. His Compendium was prized for joining brevity to completeness: nothing essential omitted, nothing needless added, the great truths of the faith set in lucid order for ready learning and use. Wollebius represents the catechetical and pedagogical genius of Reformed orthodoxy, its concern that the doctrine of grace be not only defended in the academy but taught plainly to the rising generation. He stands in the dictionary as a master of theological compression, who served the church by setting the whole counsel of God in clear and memorable order, that pastors and people might grasp and hold the faith once delivered.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Swiss Reformed theologian (1589-1629) of Basel, author of the Compendium of Christian Theology; a master of orderly compression whose concise handbook taught Reformed doctrine across Europe and early New England.

JOHANNES WOLLEBIUS, proper noun. Swiss Reformed theologian of Basel (1589-1629).

Author of the Compendium Theologiae Christianae.

A concise, orderly handbook of the whole of Reformed doctrine.

Arranged under the knowledge of God and the worship of God.

Widely used to teach theology across Europe and in early New England.

📖 Key Scripture

2 Tim 1:13 — "Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus."

Deut 6:7 — "And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up."

Luke 1:4 — "That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed."

Prov 22:6 — "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Wollebius's example honors the recovery of clear, orderly instruction in doctrine, against an age that neglects the systematic teaching of the faith and leaves believers without a form of sound words.

expand to see more

Doctrine-disordered misreading. A faith taught only in fragments and impressions leaves believers unable to hold or defend the truth. Wollebius's gift was order: he set the whole of doctrine in clear arrangement, that it might be learned, remembered, and used. The dictionary holds the value of systematic instruction — a form of sound words (2 Tim 1:13) — against a piecemeal religion that never gives the believer the shape of the faith as a whole.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the catechetical handing-on of doctrine to the next generation. Wollebius wrote not for display but for teaching, that students and children might grasp the certainty of the things they had been taught (Luke 1:4). The dictionary commends his labor of compression and clarity: the church is bound to teach its children diligently, and clear, ordered doctrine is a gift to every generation that must learn the faith anew.
